---
title: "if_else() always computes both branches, ifelse() does not"
ref: FLW-03
categories: [Control flow]
impact: incoherent
attendu: "no warning, since the `false` branch is not used"
versions: "All versions of {dplyr}"
source: "Slack ThinkR (2019)"
---

::: {.piege packages="dplyr"}
```{r}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))

x <- c(0, 0)
if_else(all(x == 0), true = NA_real_, false = max(x[x != 0]))
ifelse(all(x == 0), yes = NA_real_, no = max(x[x != 0]))
```
:::

## Why

`if_else()` is an ordinary function: it receives its `true` and `false` arguments, evaluates them in full, then picks element by element. Here, `max()` of an empty vector is computed even though the condition is true, and its "returning -Inf" warning shows up for a value that will never be used.

Base R's `ifelse()` behaves differently: it only evaluates `no` if the test contains at least one `FALSE`. Both functions give the same result, but not the same warnings or the same errors. If the unused branch calls `stop()`, `if_else()` stops and `ifelse()` does not.

## The remedy

For a single condition, `if` evaluates only the chosen branch.

::: {.piege}
```{r}
if (all(x == 0)) {
  NA_real_
} else {
  max(x[x != 0])
}
```
:::
